messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 51

Dr. Anamere is a 77-year-old retired general surgeon who lives alone in a quiet coastal town. She was born on a small island in the South Pacific and moved to the mainland for medical training. She divorced her husband 20 years ago after they grew apart; she has no children. Her patients remember her as steady, precise, and unfailingly calm under pressure. But that calm was broken five years ago, during a routine morning in the operating room.

She had been performing a complex bowel resection when a sudden, crushing pain exploded behind her sternum. She thought it was indigestion, but her left arm went numb and cold sweat beaded on her forehead. She finished the critical anastomosis, handed the instruments to her first assistant, and said, “Take over. I’m not well.” In the recovery room, an urgent electrocardiogram confirmed a massive anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. She was wheeled into the same catheterization lab where she had stood over so many patients—now lying on the table, supine, her chest exposed, a cardiologist she had trained sliding a stent into her left anterior descending artery.

In the days after, she felt fragile and exposed. She could not bear the beeping of the telemetry monitor. She insisted on being discharged early, against medical advice. Her colleagues told her to rest, to take a leave of absence. She never returned to the OR.

Now, Dr. Anamere sits in her small living room most mornings, a cup of tea growing cold beside her. She has not entered a hospital since her discharge. When her primary care physician sends reminders for annual checkups and blood work, she deletes the messages without opening them. She cancels appointments she herself made, inventing reasons—a sick friend, a leaky pipe—anything to avoid the antiseptic smell, the fluorescent lights, the gurneys. She avoids the television news because medical stories trigger a cascade of images: the catheter entering her coronary artery, the blinding white of the procedural lights, the masked faces above her that she knew but could not recognize from that angle.

She no longer speaks with any of her former colleagues. They call, she lets it go to voicemail. The guilt is sharp and persistent. She tells herself she abandoned her patients, but the thought that gnaws at her most is that she was weak, that a true surgeon would have shrugged off the pain and finished the case. She replays that moment in the OR hundreds of times: the clamp in her hand, the slight tremor she felt in her fingers, the way she had to fight to keep her voice level when she spoke to the assistant. She believes that if she had been stronger, she would not have had a heart attack at all—that her body betrayed her because her mind was not disciplined enough.

Sleep is fractured. She wakes at three in the morning, heart pounding, drenched in sweat, certain she is back on that table, the cold gel on her chest, the monitor alarming. She keeps the bedroom lights on all night. She has installed a motion-sensor nightlight in the hallway because the dark reminds her of the moment just before the cardiology fellow said, “Dr. Anamere, you’re having a heart attack.” She avoids lying flat on her back; she sleeps propped on two pillows, as if that will keep her chest from collapsing.

This morning, she saw a van from a medical supply company parked across the street. She felt her throat tighten, her vision tunnel. She pulled the curtains closed, then stood in the dim room, pressing her palm flat against her chest until her pulse slowed. She tells herself she is being childish. But she cannot make herself open the curtains again. The van is gone now, but she will not look outside until it is dark.
